prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Security advisories for affected dependencies (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "CVE ID" · longest unbreakable word 41px · one-line width 110px
  col 2: header "Package" · longest unbreakable word 144px · one-line width 144px
  col 3: header "Affected versions" · longest unbreakable word 55px · one-line width 297px
  col 4: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 52px · one-line width 52px
  col 5: header "Summary" · longest unbreakable word 195px · one-line width 2738px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 793px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 792px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Help readers identify vulnerable dependencies, assess severity, and determine whether their installed versions are affected.","reading":"Readers can scan CVE IDs, packages, and severity, then compare version ranges and read the relevant summary. Long summaries will often set row height, leaving room for version ranges to wrap within the same row.","groups":["CVE ID and Package identify the advisory and dependency.","Affected versions and Package work together to determine exposure.","Severity and Summary convey urgency and describe the issue."],"keep_intact":["CVE identifiers","Package names, including slash-separated paths","Individual version numbers and comparison operators","Severity labels"],"may_wrap":["Affected version ranges at spaces or between comma-separated ranges","Summary prose at word boundaries","The Affected versions header"]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r0A: widths [131, 165, 207, 73, 216] · table 793×1824px · row heights [33, 335, 295, 275, 275, 315, 295] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 16 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r0B: widths [131, 165, 165, 73, 258] · table 793×1502px · row heights [33, 295, 235, 214, 235, 235, 255] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 14 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r0C: widths [131, 165, 135, 73, 288] · table 793×1341px · row heights [33, 255, 214, 194, 194, 214, 235] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 12 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
